reference: GNU coreutils csplit, invoked from the runner's independent system PATH on the same fixture scripts; the runner checks expected status, stdout, stderr policy, and the resulting private file tree.
coverage: Absolute line-number split points, default byte-count output, and named output pieces.
Negative regex offsets and skip patterns.
Suffix digit width, printf suffix formats, and zero-length piece elision.
Regex repetition until no further match is found.
Failure cleanup by default and output retention with -k.
Fresh redirected stdin across repeated invocations in one shell.
exclusions: Large inputs, locale-specific regex behavior, malformed option combinations, and filesystem permission failures are outside this compact suite.
The case count exceeds the preferred range to preserve existing cases and isolate additional boundaries and regressions.

cases.purpose: Check the standard absolute line split, default byte counts, prefix naming, and complete output bytes against GNU csplit.
Check repeated regex split points while omitting each matched separator line.
Check the documented negative regex offset, which places the split before a line preceding the match.
Check a skip pattern followed by a regex split, including which lines remain in the resulting pieces.
Check -n digit width and -f prefix on output piece names.
Check GNU's printf-style suffix format on generated piece names.
Check --elide-empty-files when the first regex matches the first input line.
Check {*} repeated regex splitting through all matching separators and the final unmatched tail.
Check GNU's nonzero status and default removal of pieces after a later pattern fails.
cases.script:
printf 'one
two
three
four
' > data; set +e; csplit -s -f fail- data 3 '/^MISSING$/'; result=$?; set -e; exit "$result"

cases.purpose: Check -k retaining pieces made before and during a later pattern failure.
cases.script:
printf 'one
two
three
four
' > data; set +e; csplit -s -k -f keep- data 3 '/^MISSING$/'; result=$?; set -e; exit "$result"

cases.purpose: Check that two csplit calls in one persistent shell each read a fresh copy of the redirected input and write independent pieces.
cases.script:
printf 'one
two
three
' > data; csplit -s -f first- - 2 < data; csplit -s -f again- - 2 < data

cases.purpose: Line splits preserve embedded NUL and an unterminated final record including exact byte counts.
A missing relative input fails without output pieces.
